newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Retail investors snap up Telefonica shares.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Retail investors snap up Telefonica shares.

text.p: Retail investors scrambled to get their orders in early for stock in Spanish telecommunications group Telefonica de Espana which is being privatised with the sale of the state's remaining 20.94 percent stake.
In the first two days of the offer period, retail investors bid for 300 billion pesetas ($2.2 billion) worth of shares, press reports said, though the firm would not confirm them.
This amount would mean the original 85.54 million share allotment for the retail tranche -- which could be expanded by 10 percent -- had already been met.
On the first day of the offer, Telefonica confirmed it had received subscriptions for more than half of those in the original retail tranche for a value of 155.21 billion pesetas.
Telefonica Chairman Juan Villalonga told local radio on Wednesday that more than 200,000 offers had been received with an average investment of 400,000 to 500,000 pesetas.

Analysts said the enormous appetite for the shares was unsurprising despite initial concerns that the share's huge gains in the past year would deter investors. Telefonica shares have doubled in value since January 1995, and reached a new peak of 3,420 pesetas on Monday.
"It seems completely logical, with an operation based on the retail tranche. It doesn't surprise us that there is so much demand," an analyst at a Madrid bank said.
The Telefonica offering size is 171 million shares, or 18.2 percent of the group, with the rest reserved for over-subscriptions and bonuses for those who hold onto stock.
The domestic tranche represents 58 percent of the total offer, of which 50 percent is destined for retail investors. Telefonica said it might expand this portion to 60 percent.

Telefonica Finance Director Alfonso Pajuelo told Reuters on Monday the group was not worried about the share price rise, but he added that a reasonable price range would be between 3,300 and 3,400 and emphasised the lower end of the range.
Addressing an economic seminar in Madrid, Spanish Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato said on Wednesday that the response to the government's sale was "very satisfactory".

"Telefonica is carrying out an enormous publicity campaign and it is normal that there is so much interest, although it is still premature to talk about how the sale will come out in the end," said another analyst at a brokerage.

Telefonica, founded by U.S. operator International Telephone and Telegraph in 1924 and later nationalised, is one of Spain's most respected companies. It has said it would spend 3.3 billion pesetas promoting the sale, which ends February 18.
The home-based appetite for Telefonica has been strong ever since the late dictator Francisco Franco started building up the populist image of the company for share sales in the late 1960s.
The last privatisation of 12 percent of the firm in 1995 was 8.1 times oversubscribed all in all, with the institutional segment just under twice overbid.

Privatisation programmes in Spain in the past few years have been hugely sucessful. The offering of 10 percent of energy blue chip Repsol at the start of 1996 was eight times oversubscribed, while the sale of 25 percent of Argentaria bank in March of the same year was overbid five times.
Gas Natural, the first privatisation under the new centre-right government, was equally well-received in December, with offers outnumbering shares by more than three.
The sale of another 10 percent of Repsol is due this year.
Analysts said that the continued strong performance of Spanish financial markets provided a strong backdrop for the share offer.
"The fall in bond yields and the advance of international bourses have favoured the Telefonica placement," said one.
